Design notebook · Concept stage

Live creation
for digital sound.

The Electromechanical Drum System is an instrument I'm designing so the 808s and digital drums of modern music can be played live, by hand, with all the feeling of a real drummer behind a real kit.

Luke BurgessMechanical Engineering, University of GeorgiaIndependent project

About this page

This page shows the early design thinking behind the project I mention in my cover letter. The ideas and motivations are mine, taken from my notebook. I used generative AI (Claude) to design and build this page, type up my handwritten notes, and redraw my sketches as the cleaner diagrams and demos you'll see below.

Nothing here is technical yet and no hardware has been built. It's a look at how I'm thinking through the problem, what I'm researching on my own time, and where I want to take it.

Why

Music is magic. Watching it made is something else.

Music has always been one of the purest forms of expression. It connects people through lyric and rhythm who would never otherwise have realized their shared connection. In the '50s and '60s, rock gave a young generation a voice, and concerts became cultural gatherings where ideas and sentiments were shared among a generation. The glue was the music they came to see.

The creation of music is one of the most special human abilities. From nothing but their hands and voice, people can create rhythm and share emotion through song. Instruments amplify the experience.

Today, most of what we listen to is made in a DAW with virtual instruments. That makes sense. In the digital world you can create any sound you want, many of which no acoustic instrument can make. Digital drum machines and 808s, tuned perfectly to the key of any song, have almost no weaknesses next to an acoustic kit. Except one.

Live creation

In the '90s, grunge rock utilized loud, aggressive drums to capture its equally aggressive and combatant ethos and persona. Bands like Nirvana were unapologetically anti, with Cobain once voicing his disdain for the idea of any young person listening to the same type of music their parents do. While still thick and heavy over the studio mix, the beauty of the era was that when you went to see one of these bands perform live, you would watch the drummers bring those same drums to life in a way that could not be emotionally reciprocated through a mix. There was another level of emotion felt between performer and listener, carried by the drummer's ability to speak through their kit.

“This is what I define as live creation: the ability to bring music to life and connect with an audience in a way that simply cannot be done through a pair of headphones.”From my notebook

Digital drums can't do this. While they create enthralling sounds through a pair of headphones, there currently exists no instrument that houses all the sounds of digital 808s and also lets a player bring the same intensity and flair felt over the studio mix to a live setting.

We have more sounds available to us than at any point in history, and yet live performance often means watching one person stand in front of a track playing through speakers.

The goal

Bring digital drum sound into the acoustic world without losing live creation.

It has to evoke the same emotions as an acoustic kit and invite players to play aggressively. Essentially, I'm trying to reverse engineer an instrument that shows its work emotionally.

Defining the sound

Not a giant kick drum.

My view of what digital drums and 808s can do comes from the experimental hip-hop production of roughly 2019 to 2022, and the producers pushing it further now. They tune their 808s in a DAW and play them on a piano roll across a range of notes.

They use the 808 as a bass instrument with serious percussive attack. That versatility, aggression and melody at once, is what makes it such a culturally powerful instrument, unlike anything before it.

So the instrument has to capture both the hit and the note. A monotone kick drum would miss the whole point.

The range · Sound on

Play the 808.

Eight kinds of 808 across two octaves. Pick a sound, then play the keys with your mouse, finger or computer keyboard.

Each dot is one sound at one pitch. Keys A–K play, Z X shift octave. Headphones help: 808s sit below what most phone speakers can play.

0of 200 sounds played

The challenge

Now fit all of that on something you hit without looking.

Eight sounds times 25 pitches is already 200 notes, before slides, velocity, or the sounds producers haven't invented yet. A keyboard handles this with a long row of keys. A drum has a single surface and a player swinging at it.

Try the idea · Sound on

Hit the bullseye.

My early "Bullseye" concept in code. Each ring of the membrane is mapped to a different pitch of the 808 you picked above, so where you strike decides the note. Tap or click the rings, or focus one and press Space.

Five rings hold five notes. Playing it shows the problem I wrote down next to the original sketch: when location sets pitch, you have to aim carefully to avoid wrong notes, and that fights the urge to hit it hard.

A browser approximation of an 808, synthesized live. It's a toy for the idea, not the instrument.

Iterations

How the idea has changed.

Start with what I already know.

An acoustic-style kit with pads that detect and evaluate impact velocity, so the sound carries the emotion the drummer hits with. Everything linked to a MIDI-type control system that can change the sound of each drum on its own.

  • It already exists. This is just an electronic drum kit. So why haven't those taken off?
  • Limited by reach. Every piece has to be within arm's length, and drums take up a lot of space.
  • Limited by shape. It confines the limitless expression of digital sound to a shape we already know and are comfortable with.
Set aside

Like trying to imagine a new color.

Thinking up a new way to bring live creation to digital sound is like trying to think of a new color. Our brains revert to what we know, which is why my first ideas all looked like a drum kit.

But a new color is physically impossible to see, because our eyes can only see a set spectrum of light, and every hue in it has been named. My problem is the opposite. There's no limit to digital sound. A combination of sounds that seems purely experimental today could be the basis of a whole new genre in 20 years.

In front of me lies limitless sound, and I want to find a way to physically bring it to life.

Tap anywhere. Sound on.

Every tap is a new 808. None of them have names.

Early concept: Bullseye.

  • Angled circular membrane with the technology housed under its surface and inside the stand.
  • Sound switching controlled externally, through DJ-style controllers.
  • Location sets pitch. Different spots on the membrane give different pitch responses.

My critique: it seems unintuitive. Players would have to play carefully to avoid errant notes, which defeats the emotional connection of recklessly banging a drum.

Promising, with a learnability problem

The hardest part: mapping.

A digital keyboard keeps the exact same geometry whatever sound you play. Could the drum have one constant layout that tells you the pitch, whatever sound is loaded? Only a keyboard can really lay out the range of 808 pitches in real space, and a drum laid out like that would defeat the purpose.

Another thought: internal LEDs that outline the rings, so the mapping is visible and can change with the selected sound. More technical, and more room for problems depending on playstyle.

Mapping scales onto a round drum in a way that's natural to learn and as simple as possible is the most difficult part of the process.

Working on it now

Open problems

What I don't know yet.

The questions I'm researching on my own time, before any hardware gets built.

Membrane

What do you hit?

The material has to feel like a drum, survive aggressive playing, and still let sensors underneath read every strike.

Sensing

Reading the hit

Detecting where and how hard each strike lands, so velocity carries the drummer's emotion into the sound.

Learnability

Easy to feel

Geometry that's naturally intuitive to human movement and inviting to aggressive playstyle.

Mapping

Where are the notes?

A layout of pitches on a round surface that a player can learn, and that holds up when the loaded sound changes.

Visual feedback

Notes you can see

Lighting inside the drum that shows the current mapping without getting in the way of the performance.

Control

Changing the sound

How sound switching works mid-performance, from the player or from a DJ controlling the whole show.

The bigger picture

New-age music performance.

The drum is one piece of a stage I keep sketching: a band where every player brings digital sound to life by hand. No backing track.

Every role is live.

Strings that manipulate synths. A DJ who controls input, output and sound manipulation for every instrument, changing the instrumentation song by song. A drummer who physically plays and manipulates 808s with fills and breakdowns. A vocalist out in the crowd, connecting with people.

The vision

Meet the band.

This is the show I keep picturing: digital sound with a real person behind every note, and nobody on stage pressing play. None of these instruments exist yet, and neither do these people.
